guardianfootball.description: League to invite bids to televise all games from 2029 UK leagues expected to co-ordinate move to end blackout The Scottish Premiership has made the first move in what is expected to be a coordinated attempt from the UK’s domestic leagues to remove the Saturday afternoon broadcast blackout by inviting bids to televise all of its matches in the next rights cycle from 2029. A tender document issued by the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL) last week is understood to have given broadcasters an option to bid for live rights to all matches, including games kicking off at 3pm on Saturdays, the domestic broadcast of which is currently prohibited under Article 48 of Uefa’s statutes.…

Carrick and Fernandes held talks this week after the Portuguese criticised the tactics in the loss to Como, resulting in the midfielder being an unused substitute on Sunday. Harry Maguire took the armband but will not retain it for Saturday’s game at Chelsea, with Carrick saying “there is no decision to be made” and praising Fernandes. Continue reading...

Everton took the unusual step of announcing that Grealish’s omission was for disciplinary reasons on social media, after listing David Moyes’s team for the fourth-round tie at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The club posted on X: “Jarrad Branthwaite remains sidelined for a second successive game due to concussion protocols, while Jack Grealish is unavailable for selection due to a breach of club discipline.” Continue reading...

Yet despite Manchester United being fifth-bottom of the Premier League and Chelsea fifth-top, the Blues have performed worse this season according to Opta’s expected points model. Is there a glitch in the matrix? Has the fabled supercomputer clicked on a suspicious link? Even though the margin between their data is small, it feels unthinkable that Chelsea could be below United’s level. Continue reading...

quietus.title: Audiovisual Phantasmagoria: Highlights from Semibreve 2026
quietus.description: Pedro João Santos reports from the latest edition of Portugal’s premiere festival for experimental music, where stellar sets from Noémi Büchi, Tygapaw, Marta Salogni and more lead the way Malcolm Pardon and Gustaf Broms, photo by Adriano Ferreira Borges / Semibreve A startled Jocy de Oliveira looks out at the sea: it’s well past time the grand piano should be brought ashore. She oversees a woman playing the ivories, drifting in the tide. “What do you expect to achieve this late?”, she blurts at the walkie-talkie, wrangling with the producers of her 2005 short film, Noturno De Um Piano. What starts off as an elegant allegory – the instrument set adrift in the ocean, a metaphor for the…

quietus.title: America’s Most Offensive? Ice Cube’s Death Certificate Revisited
quietus.description: Angus Batey looks back 35 years at the 360-degree attack of one of the most creatively independent yet offensive hip hop albums ever made. First published October 2011 Classic albums are supposed to be celebrated, but Death Certificate doesn't permit unqualified responses. It's a record made by a young man as talented at needling his listeners as he was at constructing and delivering some of the angriest lyrics in the hip hop canon, and is impossible to love without qualification. If you're not offended by a significant portion of it – no matter who you are, whatever your background – you're not listening properly. Just about the only universal reaction Death Certificate generates is one…

quietus.title: Put Your Hands In The Air: English Dancing Master by Leo Chadburn & Phaedra Ensemble
quietus.description: Leo Chadburn's latest work expands outwards from a seventeenth-century manual of folk dances to a kinetic exploration of human movement, from St Vitus' chorea to raving at Castlemorton Common English Dancing Master is a dance album, but not in the sense you would usually associate with the term. There is no “succession of repetitive beats” (the phrase used by the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 to criminalise outdoor raves), ribcage splintering bass or woozy toplines. Instead, we are treated to a reticent male narrator – voiced by Leo Chadburn – and the Phaedra Ensemble in conversation with each other. In fact, it’s not really an album at all but a singular radiophonic piece…

quietus.title: Maria W Horn – Melting Pillars of Snow
quietus.description: Maria W Horn Melting Pillars of Snow Melting Pillar of Snow is a dense exploration of time and decay that feels more like a static monument than a living listening experience Melting Pillars of Snow by Maria W Horn On Melting Pillars of Snow, Swedish composer Maria W Horn attempts to map the relentless passage of time across five expansive compositions. The record sets out to chart the friction between microscopic moments and deep historical time. Yet for all its conceptual weight and formal intent, the listening experience remains curiously remote, leaving the pieces sounding like static, glass-encased dioramas which may be meticulously assembled, but are emotionally lacking in power.…

quietus.title: Coming Up for Air: Andy Stott’s Favourite Albums
quietus.description: From 80s synth pop and 90s trip hop through to mischievous, glitched-out electronics, Andy Stott talks through 13 records that hold significance to him ahead of the release of his new album, Late Loop Across a career that now spans more than two decades, Andy Stott’s name has become synonymous with a style of electronic music that is patient and understated. Early records like Passed Me By and Luxury Problems dealt in dubbed-out minimalism and hauntingly gritty chuggers, while albums like 2016’s Too Many Voices and 2019’s It Should Be Us retained some of those qualities while introducing shades of dream pop into his captivating oeuvre. On new record Late Loop, which is his first studio LP…

quietus.title: Dis Fig – What To Make Of These Mortal Hands
quietus.description: Dis Fig What To Make Of These Mortal Hands Her debut was called PURGE and it was about her. This one is about what people do to each other, and it is named after the part of the body that does it What To Make Of These Mortal Hands by Dis Fig The title tells you where to look. Hands make things and hands wreck them, and Felicia Chen has built her second solo album around that double function. Track ten is called ‘A Hundred Hands’. Track six is ‘The Snake You Built’. The third track is named after the psaltery, an instrument you have to pluck with your fingers to make a sound at all. None of this is decoration. What To Make...

quietus.title: Prepared for the Future: the Slow Reveal of Aphex Twin’s Drukqs
quietus.description: Drukqs has long been one of John Doran's favourite LPs; with a reissue looming, he attempts to articulate why he loves this critically derided album so much Drukqs by Aphex Twin Rereading the contemporary reviews of Drukqs 25 years later is like rubbernecking the aftermath of a motorway crash. Just ahead of release in October 2001, it became wince-inducingly clear that some previously long-term supporters of Richard D. James were ready to start questioning the validity of his art if not gearing up to fully turn on him. His traditional allies in the leftfield press hated the album, that much was clear. “Too much cake and no nuts” was the stinging but memorable summary minted by Rob Young…

quietus.title: Nik Colk Void and More to Play Soho Electronic 2026
quietus.description: The festival of leftfield electronic music returns to Central London next month for its second edition Soho Electronic, the Central London festival championing leftfield electronic music, will return for its second edition next month. More than 30 artists are scheduled to play across four stages on and around Dean Street, with the likes of Nik Colk Void and Mark Van Hoen, otherwise known as Locust, set to make appearances. The festival will also host sets from reel-to-reel tape manipulator Howlround, Sculpture, Sonny E (FKA Adamski) and Agnes Haus, in addition to our very own Reviews Editor, Bobby Barry. Alongside the aforementioned acts, the full lineup includes live sets from Axon, Death…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Sam Gendel :: Advanced White Trash
aquariumdrunkard.description: In his classic book Mythologies, French thinker Roland Barthes criticizes plastic because it can be molded into anything—cheap, colorful surfaces open to infinite transformation. Contemporary pop is made of the same stuff, and Sam Gendel’s Advanced White Trash makes the case for what’s beautiful, even freeing, about it. The record sounds like something that was uploaded to SoundCloud at 3 a.m., a Roland Sound Canvas emulator buffering on a dying phone someone found in a Walmart parking lot, and still it comes out strangely appealing, almost hypnotic.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Ana Palindrome :: A MAN A CURE
aquariumdrunkard.description: Cork trio Ana Palindrome make a hypnotic blend of art-pop, droning vocals, sawing fiddle, and glitchy folktronica on “A MAN A CURE,” their first release for London’s World of Echo. Beneath its pulsing rhythms and woozy electronics, the track questions the idea of self-made identity, as Niamh Dalton’s voice shifts between the organic and the artificial.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Aquarium Drunkard Show (The Halloween Edition)
aquariumdrunkard.description: Trick or treat. Broadcasting from the Hollywood Forever Cemetery … The Aquarium Drunkard Show. The Halloween edition, Wednesday night / 7pm California time. SIRIUS/XM ~ Channel 35.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Boards of Canada :: Hi Scores
aquariumdrunkard.description: Earlier this year, Boards of Canada unexpectedly released their fifth album Inferno , a case of an influential artist demonstrating that their style remains eminently relatable in 2026 a.d. To close out the year, the group has dipped into its archives, re-releasing the 1996 EP Hi Scores . There’s plenty to savor here, especially for longtime BOC listeners, but there’s also something compelling about being able to hear the group’s roots in such close temporal proximity to their current venture.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Shabazz Palaces
aquariumdrunkard.description: Our guest this week on the show, Ishmael Butler of Shabazz Palaces and Digable Planets, is used to swimming in waters where science fiction weirdness and musical expression mingle. Shabazz Palaces' new album, It’s a Style Sport , represents a new high water mark for the Seattle-based rapper; at once memoiristic and mystical, it’s a strange and beguiling listen. This week, he joins Transmissions host Jason P. Woodbury to discuss basketball, his "Afro-fractal" artistic approach, the influence of artists like the Cocteau Twins, and of course, that goofy old standby: what's it like being a middle aged guy in rap?

aquariumdrunkard.title: All Hallows’ Aquarium Drunkard III
aquariumdrunkard.description: The music of autumn comes in many shades, but none of them without a little smoke and shadow. The days are growing shorter, the air a little cooler, and it is once again time to light the jack-o-lanterns. In our third installment of All Hallows' Aquarium Drunkard , the writers reveal the secrets of their spooky season soundtracks. Inside you'll find doomed teenagers, dissociative episodes, ghost planets, grisly murders and all sorts of monsters, real and imagined. Whatever kind of menace you are looking for, we've got you covered.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Willis Alan Ramsey :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: More than 50 years after releasing one of the great cult albums of the early ’70s, Willis Alan Ramsey remains an enigma: a singular songwriter whose long-awaited second record has yet to materialize. But as a recent live appearance and a first-ever vinyl reissue of his self-titled debut attest, Ramsey is very much still here — and already thinking beyond the follow-up he once abandoned. We caught up with the Texas songwriter to talk about the making of a classic, the decades since, and the music still to come.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Surprise Chef :: Frogs In A Pond
aquariumdrunkard.description: Like the best giallo scores, Surprise Chef's Frogs In A Pond finds beauty in the uneasy marriage of the sinister and the seductive. Its analog warmth and locked-in grooves evoke a bygone era without becoming trapped in it, blurring the line between recordings from 2026 and 1976. The eerie mood of the compositions, mixed with the 8-track recording, creates an auditory twilight zone that’s both nostalgic and immediate.

In her memoir, Varda par Agnès , the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe ( Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex ), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two…

A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions. nplusone.title: Playing Roulette in the Archives
nplusone.description: When Ginzburg first started his research into the witch trials, his hypothesis was that they could be seen as “a crude form of class struggle.” He swiftly found good evidence for his theory—and was disappointed. There must be something wrong, he thought, with a hypothesis that can be demonstrated so quickly: To find only what you are looking for is to learn nothing at all.

nplusone.title: Trump’s Microphones
nplusone.description: Trump is alone, photographed from below (presumably by a crouching photographer, though I never see one on the ground) so as to appear more monumental. More often than not, his arms are half-raised at his sides and his palms are up, like he’s fending off the press, rhetorically, with his habitual “Who, me?” gesture. He is encircled by a panoply of black shapes jutting in, which evokes cartoon compositions where the main character is overwhelmingly surrounded, by knives, or the Feds, or meddling kids.

nplusone.title: EV Listening
nplusone.description: The Honda Prologue has a hovering, suffusing melody, with a low rhythmic pulse and a subtle, epiphanic wash. It sounds like a computer game lifting you into heaven, or the arrival of benevolent extraterrestrial colonists. The Porsche Taycan makes a more sinister and comic, gulping, warp-speed sound, and the Nissan Ariya gives off a disturbed digital whine, like the tantrums of a petulant robot.
